title: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60

metadata.title: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60

summary: Bob Brackett explains why near-term oil cash flows, forward curves and producer equities can diverge. He favors disciplined commodity exposure, dry-gas producers, Exxon, Diamondback and Cheniere while remaining tactically cautious on copper. Eisman adopts a cyclical entry-and-exit framework. Primary evidence supports severe supply disruption, regional gas congestion and strong producer cash generation, but several long-run scenarios remain unfinished and the storage-cost explanation has the wrong sign.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Bob Brackett. Most sector models and preferences are Brackett. Eisman’s closing recap begins around 4860 seconds.
framework_points: Separate transit flows, shut-ins, inventory draws and net deficits.
Value equities on cash flows and capital allocation, not spot commodities alone.
Futures prices combine expectations, carry, convenience yield and risk premia.
Distinguish resource estimates from commercially recoverable low-cost supply.
Compare integrated, upstream, service and midstream risk separately.
Strong demand growth can coexist with poor supplier returns when capacity overexpands.
tools_and_charts: Commodity EBITDA sensitivity and net-debt bridge.
Gas basis, pipeline constraints and associated supply.
FCF yields and LNG contracted capacity.
transcript_cautions: Full audio-caption transcript read through 4981 seconds despite announced video-feed loss.
Caption confusion between growth and value indexing is resolved by the immediately following correction, not graded as a separate claim.
The briefly misstated gas-to-solid conversion is immediately corrected to liquid and not separately scored.
Guest forecasts are not assigned to Eisman; his closing recap is separately captured.

assumptions: Initial revenue is 100 and EBITDA is 50.

evidence_basis.proof: Initial costs are 50. New EBITDA is 150 minus 50, or 100, double the original 50. Royalties, taxes, fuel costs, hedges and volume changes can reduce actual sensitivity.

evidence.title: Implications of WTI futures backwardation amid the supply crunch
evidence.finding: Explains that storage, insurance and financing costs contribute to contango; backwardation reflects convenience yield exceeding carrying costs. Since 1985, front versus six-month WTI was in contango about 42% of the time and backwardation 58%.

claims.next_check: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

claims.claim: Cheap-to-store commodities tend toward contango, whereas expensive-to-store oil and iron ore tend toward backwardation because of storage cost.
claims.speaker: Bob Brackett
claims.test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.
claims.reason: The storage-cost sign is reversed when other factors are held fixed. Carrying costs raise deferred prices; backwardation requires sufficiently strong convenience yield or other forces. Oil is not almost always backwardated.

assumptions: A storable commodity with financing rate r, proportional storage cost u and convenience yield y.
evidence_basis.proof: The carry relationship is F = S exp((r + u - y)T). Increasing storage cost u raises F relative to S, pushing toward contango, not backwardation.

assumptions: A storable commodity with financing rate r, proportional storage cost u and convenience yield y.
